{{short description|Finite element method for Navier-Stokes equations}}
The '''streamline upwind Petrov–Galerkin pressure-stabilizing Petrov–Galerkin formulation for incompressible Navier–Stokes equations''' can be used for [[finite element]] computations of high [[Reynolds number]] [[incompressible flow]] using equal order of finite element space (i.e. <math> \mathbb{P}_k-\mathbb{P}_k </math>) by introducing additional stabilization terms in the Navier–Stokes [[Galerkin method|Galerkin formulation]].<ref name="Tezduyar91">{{cite journal|author-link1=Tayfun Tezduyar |last1=Tezduyar |first1=T. E. |title=Stabilized Finite Element Formulations for Incompressible Flow Computations††This research was sponsored by NASA-Johnson Space Center (under grant NAG 9-449), NSF (under grant MSM-8796352), U.S. Army (under contract DAAL03-89-C-0038), and the University of Paris VI. |journal=Advances in Applied Mechanics |date=1 January 1991 |volume=28 |pages=1–44 |publisher=Elsevier|doi=10.1016/S0065-2156(08)70153-4 }}</ref><ref name="Tobiska91">{{cite journal |last1=Tobiska |first1=Lutz |last2=Lube |first2=Gert |title=A modified streamline diffusion method for solving the stationary Navier–Stokes equation |journal=Numerische Mathematik |date=1 December 1991 |volume=59 |issue=1 |pages=13–29 |doi=10.1007/BF01385768 |s2cid=123397636 |language=en |issn=0945-3245}}</ref>

The finite element (FE) numerical computation of incompressible [[Navier–Stokes equations]] (NS) suffers from two main sources of numerical [[Numerical stability|instabilities]] arising from the associated Galerkin problem.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/> Equal order finite elements for [[pressure]] and [[velocity]], (for example, <math> \mathbb{P}_k-\mathbb{P}_k, \; \forall k \ge 0 </math>), do not satisfy the [[inf-sup condition]] and leads to instability on the discrete pressure (also called spurious pressure).<ref name="Tobiska91"/>
Moreover, the [[advection]] term in the Navier–Stokes equations can produce [[oscillation]]s in the velocity field (also called spurious velocity).<ref name="Tobiska91"/> Such spurious velocity oscillations become more evident for advection-dominated (i.e., high [[Reynolds number]] <math> Re </math>) flows.<ref name="Tobiska91"/> To control instabilities arising from inf-sup condition and convection dominated problem, pressure-stabilizing Petrov–Galerkin (PSPG) stabilization along with Streamline-Upwind Petrov-Galerkin (SUPG) stabilization can be added to the NS Galerkin formulation.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/><ref name="Tobiska91"/>

==The incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for a Newtonian fluid==

Let <math> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3 </math> be the spatial [[fluid]] domain with a smooth [[Boundary (topology)|boundary]] <math> \partial \Omega \equiv \Gamma </math>, where <math> \Gamma=\Gamma_N \cup \Gamma_D </math> with <math> \Gamma_D </math> the subset of <math> \Gamma </math> in which the essential ([[Dirichlet boundary condition|Dirichlet]]) [[boundary conditions]] are set, while <math> \Gamma_N </math> the portion of the boundary where natural ([[Neumann boundary condition|Neumann]]) boundary conditions have been considered. Moreover, <math> \Gamma_N = \Gamma \setminus \Gamma_D </math>, and <math> \Gamma_N \cap \Gamma_D=\emptyset </math>. Introducing an unknown velocity field <math> \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t):\Omega \times [0,T] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 </math> and an unknown pressure field <math> p(\mathbf{x},t):\Omega \times [0,T] \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math>, in absence of [[body forces]], the [[Incompressible flow|incompressible]] Navier–Stokes (NS) equations read<ref name="Quarteroni14">{{cite book |author-link1= Alfio Quarteroni |last1=Quarteroni |first1=Alfio |title=Numerical Models for Differential Problems |date=2014 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-88-470-5883-5 |edition=2 |url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9788847058835 |language=en}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}+( \mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u - \frac{1}{\rho}\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma} (\mathbf u,p)=\mathbf 0 & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],
\\
\nabla \cdot {\mathbf u}=0 & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],
\\
\mathbf u = \mathbf g & \text{on } \Gamma_D \times (0,T],
\\
\boldsymbol{\sigma} (\mathbf u,p) \mathbf{\hat{n}} = \mathbf h & \text{on } \Gamma_N \times (0,T],
\\
\mathbf{u} (\mathbf{x},0) = \mathbf u_0(\mathbf{x})& \text{in } \Omega \times \{0\},
\end{cases}</math>
where <math> \mathbf{\hat{n}} </math> is the outward directed unit [[normal vector]] to <math> \Gamma_N </math>, <math> \boldsymbol{\sigma} </math> is the [[Cauchy stress tensor]], <math> \rho </math> is the fluid [[density]] , and <math> \nabla </math> and <math> \nabla \cdot </math> are the usual [[gradient]] and [[divergence]] [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]]s.
The functions <math> \mathbf g </math> and <math> \mathbf h </math> indicate suitable Dirichlet and Neumann data, respectively, while <math> \mathbf u_0 </math> is the known initial field [[Partial differential equation|solution]] at time <math> t=0 </math>.

For a [[Newtonian fluid]], the Cauchy stress tensor <math> \boldsymbol{\sigma} </math> depends linearly on the components of the [[strain rate tensor]]:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\sigma} (\mathbf u,p)=-p \mathbf{I} +2\mu \mathbf S(\mathbf u),</math>
where <math> \mu </math> is the [[dynamic viscosity]] of the fluid (taken to be a known constant) and <math> \mathbf{I} </math> is the second order [[tensor|identity tensor]], while <math> \mathbf S(\mathbf u) </math> is the [[strain rate tensor]]
<math display="block">\mathbf S(\mathbf u)=\frac{1}{2} \big[ \nabla \mathbf u + (\nabla \mathbf u)^T \big].</math>

The first of the NS equations represents the [[Momentum|balance of the momentum]] and the second one the conservation of the mass, also called [[continuity equation]] (or incompressible constraint).<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> [[Vector-valued function|Vectorial functions]] <math> \mathbf u_0 </math>, <math> \mathbf g </math>, and <math> \mathbf h </math> are assigned.

Hence, the [[strong formulation]] of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for a constant density, Newtonian and [[Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures|homogeneous fluid]] can be written as:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Find, <math> \forall t \in (0,T] </math>, velocity <math> \mathbf u(\mathbf{x},t) </math> and pressure <math> p(\mathbf{x},t) </math> such that:
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}+( \mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u + \nabla \hat p -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u)=\mathbf 0 & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],
\\
\nabla \cdot {\mathbf u}=0 & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],
\\
\left( - \hat p \mathbf{I} +2\nu \mathbf S(\mathbf u) \right) \mathbf{\hat{n}} = \mathbf h & \text{on } \Gamma_N \times (0,T],
\\
\mathbf u = \mathbf g & \text{on } \Gamma_D \times (0,T] \;,
\\
\mathbf{u} (\mathbf{x},0) = \mathbf u_0(\mathbf{x}) & \text{in } \Omega \times \{0\},
\end{cases}</math>
where, <math> \nu = \frac{\mu}{\rho} </math> is the [[kinematic viscosity]], and <math> \hat p=\frac{p}{\rho} </math> is the pressure rescaled by density (however, for the sake of clearness, the hat on pressure variable will be neglect in what follows).

In the NS equations, the Reynolds number shows how important is the non linear term, <math> ( \mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u </math>, compared to the dissipative term, <math> \nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u):</math><ref name="Pope2000">{{cite book |last1=Pope |first1=Stephen B. |title=Turbulent Flows by Stephen B. Pope |date=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-59886-6 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/turbulent-flows/69322053C06F73F7EB7124915F9256BD |language=en}}</ref>
<math display="block">
\frac{( \mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u}{\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u)}\approx \frac{\frac{U^2}{L}}{\nu\frac{U}{L^2}}=\frac{UL}{\nu} = \mathrm{Re}.
</math>

The Reynolds number is a measure of the ratio between the [[advection]] [[convection]] terms, generated by [[inertia]]l forces in the [[flow velocity]], and the [[diffusion]] term specific of fluid [[viscous forces]].<ref name="Pope2000"/> Thus, <math> \mathrm{Re} </math> can be used to discriminate between advection-convection dominated flow and diffusion dominated one.<ref name="Pope2000"/> Namely:
* for "low" <math> \mathrm{Re} </math>, viscous forces dominate and we are in the viscous fluid situation (also named [[Laminar Flow]]),<ref name="Pope2000"/>
* for "high" <math> \mathrm{Re} </math>, inertial forces prevail and a slightly viscous fluid with high velocity emerges (also named [[Turbulent Flow]]).<ref name="Pope2000"/>

===The weak formulation of the Navier–Stokes equations===
The [[weak formulation]] of the strong formulation of the NS equations is obtained by multiplying the first two NS equations by [[test functions]] <math> \mathbf v </math> and <math> q </math>, respectively, belonging to suitable [[function spaces]], and integrating these equation all over the fluid domain <math> \Omega </math>.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> As a consequence:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}\cdot \mathbf v\,d\Omega+ \int_{\Omega}(\mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega + \int_{\Omega}\nabla p \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega\,-\int_{\Omega}2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u) \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega = 0,
\\
& \int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf u \, q \,d\Omega=0. 
\end{align} </math>

By summing up the two equations and performing [[integration by parts]] for pressure (<math> \nabla p </math>) and viscous (<math> \nabla \cdot \mathbf S (\mathbf u) </math>) term:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">\int_\Omega \frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}\cdot \mathbf v\,d\Omega+ \int_{\Omega}(\mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega\,
+\int_\Omega \nabla \cdot \mathbf u \, q \,d\Omega- \int_{\Omega}p \nabla \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega+\int_{\partial \Omega}p \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf{\hat n} \,d\Gamma \,
+ \int_\Omega 2\nu \mathbf S(\mathbf u) : \nabla \mathbf v \,d\Omega-\int_{\partial \Omega}2\nu \mathbf S(\mathbf u) \cdot \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf{\hat n} \,d\Gamma \, =0. </math>

Regarding the choice of the function spaces, it's enough that <math> p </math> and <math> q </math>, <math> \mathbf u </math> and <math> \mathbf v </math>, and their [[derivative]], <math> \nabla \mathbf u </math> and <math> \nabla \mathbf v </math> are [[square-integrable functions]] in order to have sense in the [[integral]]s that appear in the above formulation.<ref name="Quarteroni14" /> Hence,<ref name="Quarteroni14" />
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \mathcal{Q} = L^2(\Omega) = \left\{ q \in \Omega \text{ s.t. } \Vert q\Vert_{L^2}=\sqrt{\int_{\Omega}{\vert q \vert^2 \ d\Omega}} < \infty \right\},
\\
& \mathcal{V}=\{ \mathbf v \in [L^2(\Omega)]^3 \text{ and } \nabla \mathbf v \in [L^2(\Omega)]^{3 \times 3}, \, \mathbf v|_{\Gamma_{D}}=\mathbf g \},
\\ 
& \mathcal{V}_0=\{ \mathbf v \in \mathcal{V} \text{ s.t. } \mathbf v|_{\Gamma_D}=\mathbf 0\}. 
\end{align} </math>

Having specified the function spaces <math> \mathcal{V} </math>, <math> \mathcal{V}_0 </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q} </math>, and by applying the boundary conditions, the boundary terms can be rewritten as<ref name="Quarteroni14" />
<math display="block">
\int_{\Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_N}p \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf{\hat n} \,d\Gamma+ \int_{\Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_N} -2\nu S(\mathbf u) \cdot \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf{\hat n} \,d\Gamma,
</math>
where <math> \partial \Omega=\Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_N </math>. The integral terms with <math> \Gamma_D </math> vanish because <math> \mathbf v|_{\Gamma_D}=\mathbf 0 </math>, while the term on <math> \Gamma_N </math> become
<math display="block">
\int_{\Gamma_{N}} [p \mathbf I -2\nu S(\mathbf u)] \cdot \mathbf v \cdot \mathbf{\hat n} \,d\Gamma = -\int_{\Gamma_{N}} \mathbf h \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Gamma,
</math>

The weak formulation of Navier–Stokes equations reads:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Find, for all <math> t \in (0,T] </math>, <math> (\mathbf u,p)\in \{ \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{Q}\} </math>, such that
<math display="block"> \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t},\mathbf v \right)+c(\mathbf u,\mathbf u,\mathbf v)+b(\mathbf u,q)-b(\mathbf v,p) + a(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) = f(\mathbf v)</math>

with <math> \mathbf{u}|_{t=0}=\mathbf{u}_0 </math>, where<ref name="Quarteroni14" />
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\left( \frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t},\mathbf v \right)&:=\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}\cdot \mathbf v\,d\Omega,
\\ 
b(\mathbf u,q)&:=\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf u \, q \,d\Omega,
\\
a(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)&:=\int_{\Omega}2\nu \mathbf S(\mathbf u) : \nabla \mathbf v \,d\Omega,
\\
c(\mathbf w,\mathbf u,\mathbf v)&:=\int_{\Omega}(\mathbf w \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Omega,
\\
f(\mathbf v)&:=-\int_{\Gamma_{N}} \mathbf h \cdot \mathbf v \,d\Gamma.
\end{align} </math>

==Finite element Galerkin formulation of Navier–Stokes equations==

In order to numerically solve the NS problem, first the [[discretization]] of the weak formulation is performed.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
Consider a [[triangulation]] <math> \Omega_h </math>, composed by [[tetrahedra]] <math> \mathcal{T}_i </math>, with <math> i = 1, \ldots, N_{\mathcal{T}} </math> (where <math> N_{\mathcal{T}} </math> is the total number of tetrahedra), of the domain <math> \Omega </math> and <math> h </math> is the [[characteristic length]] of the element of the triangulation.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Introducing two families of [[Linear subspace|finite-dimensional sub-spaces]] <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math>, approximations of <math> \mathcal{V} </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q} </math> respectively, and depending on a discretization parameter <math> h </math>, with <math> \dim \mathcal{V}_h = N_V </math> and <math> \dim \mathcal{Q}_h = N_Q </math>,<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\mathcal{V}_h \subset \mathcal{V} \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \mathcal{Q}_h \subset \mathcal{Q},
</math>
the discretized-in-space Galerkin problem of the weak NS equation reads:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Find, for all <math> t \in (0,T] </math>, <math> (\mathbf u_h,p_h)\in \{ \mathcal{V}_{h} \times \mathcal{Q}_h\} </math>, such that
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf u_h}{\partial t},\mathbf v_h \right)+c(\mathbf u_h,\mathbf u_h,\mathbf v_h)+b(\mathbf u_h,q_h)-b(\mathbf v_h,p_h)+a(\mathbf u_h,\mathbf v_h)=f(\mathbf v_h)
\\
& \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\forall \mathbf v_h \in \mathcal{V}_{0h} \;\;,\;\; \forall q_h \in \mathcal{Q}_h, 
\end{align}</math>
with <math> \mathbf{u}_h|_{t=0}=\mathbf{u}_{h,0} </math>, where <math> \mathbf{g}_{h} </math> is the [[approximation]] (for example, its [[interpolant]]) of <math> \mathbf{g} </math>, and
<math display="block">\mathcal{V}_{0h}=\{ \mathbf v_h \in \mathcal{V}_h \text{ s.t. } \mathbf v_h|_{\Gamma_D}=\mathbf 0\}.</math>

Time discretization of discretized-in-space NS Galerkin problem can be performed, for example, by using the second order [[Backward Differentiation Formula]] (BDF2), that is an [[Explicit and implicit methods|implicit]] second order [[multistep method]].<ref name="Quarteroni07">{{cite book |author-link1= Alfio Quarteroni |last1=Quarteroni |first1=Alfio |last2=Sacco |first2=Riccardo |last3=Saleri |first3=Fausto |title=Numerical Mathematics |date=2007 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-3-540-34658-6 |edition=2 |url=https://www.springer.com/de/book/9783540346586 |language=en}}</ref> Divide uniformly the finite [[time interval]] <math> [0,T] </math> into <math> N_t </math> [[time step]] of size <math> \delta t</math><ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">t_n=n\delta t, \;\;\; n=0,1,2,\ldots,N_t \;\;\;\;\; N_t=\frac{T}{\delta t}.</math>

For a general function <math> z </math>, denoted by <math> z^n </math> as the approximation of <math> z(t_n) </math>. Thus, the BDF2 approximation of the [[time derivative]] reads as follows:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\left( \frac{\partial \mathbf u_h}{\partial t} \right)^{n+1} \simeq \frac{ 3 \mathbf u_h^{n+1} -4 \mathbf u_h^{n}+ \mathbf u_h^{n-1}}{2\delta t} \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{for } n \geq 1.
</math>

So, the fully discretized in time and space NS Galerkin problem is:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Find, for <math> n = 0, 1, \ldots, N_t-1 </math>, <math> (\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,p^{n+1}_h)\in \{ \mathcal{V}_{h} \times \mathcal{Q}_h\} </math>, such that
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\left( \frac{ 3 \mathbf u_h^{n+1} -4 \mathbf u_h^{n}+ \mathbf u_h^{n-1}}{2\delta t},\mathbf v_h \right) & + c(\mathbf u^*_h,\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,\mathbf v_h)+b(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,q_h)-b(\mathbf v_h,p_h^{n+1})+ a(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,\mathbf v_h)=f(\mathbf v_h),
\\
& \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\forall \mathbf v_h \in \mathcal{V}_{0h} \;\;,\;\; \forall q_h \in \mathcal{Q}_h, 
\end{align}</math>
with <math> \mathbf{u}^{0}_h = \mathbf{u}_{h,0} </math>, and <math> \mathbf{u}^*_h </math> is a quantity that will be detailed later in this section.

The main issue of a fully implicit method for the NS Galerkin formulation is that the resulting problem is still [[Nonlinear partial differential equation|non linear]], due to the [[Convection|convective term]], <math> c(\mathbf u^*_h,\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,\mathbf v_h)</math>.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> Indeed, if <math> \mathbf{u}^*_h=\mathbf{u}^{n+1}_h </math> is put, this choice leads to solve a non-linear system (for example, by means of the [[Newton's method|Newton]] or [[Fixed-point iteration|Fixed point]] algorithm) with a huge computational cost.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> In order to reduce this cost, it is possible to use a [[Semi-implicit Euler method|semi-implicit]] approach with a second order [[extrapolation]] for the velocity, <math> \mathbf u^*_h </math>, in the convective term:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">\mathbf u^*_h=2\mathbf u^{n}_h-\mathbf u^{n-1}_h.</math>However, the time steps need to be smaller with the second-order extrapolation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kadapa |first=Chennakesava |last2=Dettmer |first2=Wulf G. |last3=Perić |first3=Djordje |date=2020-08-01 |title=Accurate iteration-free mixed-stabilised formulation for laminar incompressible Navier–Stokes: Applications to fluid–structure interaction |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0889974619309612 |journal=Journal of Fluids and Structures |volume=97 |article-number=103077 |doi=10.1016/j.jfluidstructs.2020.103077 |issn=0889-9746|arxiv=2001.04925 }}</ref> An alternative is to use a linearised version of the convection term:<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">c(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, \mathbf u^{n+1}_h, \mathbf v_h)
\approx
c(\mathbf u^{n}_h, \mathbf u^{n+1}_h, \mathbf v_h)
+
c(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, \mathbf u^{n}_h, \mathbf v_h)
-c(\mathbf u^{n}_h, \mathbf u^{n}_h, \mathbf v_h).</math>

===Finite element formulation and the INF-SUP condition===
Let's define the finite element (FE) spaces of [[continuous functions]], <math> X_h^r </math> ([[polynomials]] of degree <math> r </math> on each element <math> \mathcal{T}_i </math> of the triangulation) as<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
X_h^r= \left\{ v_h \in C^0(\overline{\Omega}) : v_h|_{\mathcal{T}_i} \in \mathbb{P}_r \ \forall \mathcal{T}_i \in \Omega_h \right\} \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; r=0,1,2,\ldots,
</math>
where, <math> \mathbb{P}_r </math> is the space of polynomials of degree less than or equal to <math> r </math>.

Introduce the finite element formulation, as a specific Galerkin problem, and choose <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math> as<ref name="Quarteroni14" />
<math display="block">
\mathcal{V}_h\equiv [X_h^r]^3 \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \mathcal{Q}_h\equiv X_h^s \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; r,s \in \mathbb{N}.
</math>

The FE spaces <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math> need to satisfy the [[Ladyzhenskaya–Babuška–Brezzi condition|inf-sup condition]](or LBB):<ref name="Brezzi91">{{cite book |title=Mixed and Hybrid Finite Element Methods |volume=15 |date=1991 |language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-3172-1 |series=Springer Series in Computational Mathematics |isbn=978-1-4612-7824-5 |last1=Brezzi |first1=Franco |last2=Fortin |first2=Michel |url= https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00075815/file/RR-0737.pdf}}<!--https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00075815/file/RR-0737.pdf--></ref>
<math display="block">
\exists \beta_h >0 \;\text{ s.t. } \; \inf_{q_h \in \mathcal{Q}_h}\sup_{\mathbf v_h \in \mathcal{V}_h} \frac{b(q_h,\mathbf v_h)}{\Vert \mathbf v_h \Vert_{H^1} \Vert q_h \Vert_{L^2}} \geq \beta_h \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \forall h>0,
</math>

with <math> \beta_h >0 </math>, and independent of the [[mesh]] size <math> h.</math><ref name="Brezzi91" /> This [[Property (mathematics)|property]] is necessary for the [[Well-posed problem|well posedness]] of the discrete problem and the [[Numerical method|optimal convergence of the method]].<ref name="Brezzi91" /> Examples of FE spaces satisfying the inf-sup condition are the so named Taylor-Hood pair <math> \mathbb{P}_{k+1}-\mathbb{P}_k </math> (with <math> k \geq 1 </math>), where it can be noticed that the velocity space <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> has to be, in some sense, "richer" in comparison to the pressure space <math> \mathcal{Q}_h. </math><ref name="Brezzi91" /> Indeed, the inf-sup condition couples the space <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math>, and it is a sort of compatibility condition between the velocity and pressure spaces.<ref name="Brezzi91" />

The equal order finite elements, <math> \mathbb{P}_{k}-\mathbb{P}_k </math> (<math> \forall k </math>), do not satisfy the inf-sup condition and leads to instability on the discrete pressure (also called spurious pressure).<ref name="Brezzi91" /> However, <math> \mathbb{P}_{k}-\mathbb{P}_k </math> can still be used with additional stabilization terms such as Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin with a Pressure-Stabilizing Petrov-Galerkin term (SUPG-PSPG).<ref name="Tobiska91" /><ref name="Tezduyar91" />

In order to derive the FE [[Algebraic equation|algebraic formulation]] of the fully discretized Galerkin NS problem, it is necessary to introduce two [[Basis function|basis]] for the discrete spaces <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math><ref name="Quarteroni14" />
<math display="block">\{ \boldsymbol{\phi}_i(\mathbf x) \}_{i=1}^{N_V} \;\;\;\;\;\; \{ \psi_k(\mathbf x) \}_{k=1}^{N_Q},</math>
in order to expand our [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]] as<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">\mathbf u^n_h = \sum_{j=1}^{N_V} U^n_j \boldsymbol{\phi}_j(\mathbf x), \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; q^n_h=\sum_{l=1}^{N_Q} P^n_l \psi_l(\mathbf x).</math>

The [[coefficient]]s, <math> U^n_j </math> (<math> j=1,\ldots,N_V </math>) and <math> P^n_l </math> (<math> l=1,\ldots,N_Q </math>) are called [[degrees of freedom]] (d.o.f.) of the finite element for the velocity and pressure field, respectively. The [[dimension]] of the FE spaces, <math> N_V </math> and <math> N_Q </math>, is the number of d.o.f, of the velocity and pressure field, respectively. Hence, the total number of d.o.f <math> N_{d.o.f} </math> is <math> N_{d.o.f}=N_V+N_Q </math>.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>

Since the fully discretized Galerkin problem holds for all elements of the space <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> and <math> \mathcal{Q}_h </math>, then it is valid also for the basis.<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> Hence, choosing these basis functions as test functions in the fully discretized NS Galerkin problem, and using [[bilinearity]] of <math> a(\cdot,\cdot) </math> and <math> b(\cdot,\cdot) </math>, and [[Multilinear form|trilinearity]] of <math> c(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot) </math>, the following linear system is obtained:<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle M \frac{ 3 \mathbf U^{n+1} -4 \mathbf U^{n}+ \mathbf U^{n-1}}{2\delta t} + A\mathbf U^{n+1} +C(\mathbf U^*)\mathbf U^{n+1}+\displaystyle{B^T \mathbf P^{n+1} = \mathbf F^{n}}
\\
\displaystyle{B \mathbf U^{n+1} = \mathbf 0}
\end{cases}
</math>
where <math> M \in \mathbb{R}^{N_V \times N_V} </math> , <math> A \in \mathbb{R}^{N_V \times N_V} </math>, <math> C(\mathbf U^*) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_V \times N_V} </math>, <math> B \in \mathbb{R}^{N_Q \times N_V} </math>, and <math> F \in \mathbb{R}^{N_V} </math> are given by<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
& M_{ij}=\int_{\Omega} \boldsymbol{\phi}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\phi}_i d\Omega
\\
& A_{ij}=a(\boldsymbol{\phi}_j,\boldsymbol{\phi}_i)
\\
& C_{ij}(\mathbf u^*)=c(\mathbf u^*,\boldsymbol{\phi}_j,\boldsymbol{\phi}_i),
\\
& B_{kj}=b(\boldsymbol{\phi}_j,\psi_k),
\\
& F_{i}=f(\boldsymbol{\phi}_i)
\end{align}
</math>
and <math> \mathbf U </math> and <math> \mathbf P </math> are the unknown vectors<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\mathbf U^n=\Big( U^n_1,\ldots,U^n_{N_V} \Big)^T, \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \mathbf P^n=\Big( P^n_1,\ldots,P^n_{N_Q} \Big)^T.
</math>

Problem is completed by an [[initial condition]] on the velocity <math> \mathbf U(0)=\mathbf U_0 </math>. Moreover, using the semi-implicit treatment <math> \mathbf U^{*}=2\mathbf U^{n}-\mathbf U^{n-1} </math>, the trilinear term <math> c(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot) </math> becomes bilinear, and the corresponding [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] is<ref name="Quarteroni14"/> 
<math display="block">
C_{ij}=c(\mathbf u^*,\boldsymbol{\phi}_j,\boldsymbol{\phi}_i)=\int_{\Omega}(\mathbf u^* \cdot \nabla ) \boldsymbol{\phi}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\phi}_i \,d\Omega,
</math>

Hence, the [[linear system]] can be written in a single [[Monolithic system|monolithic]] matrix (<math> \Sigma </math>, also called monolithic NS matrix) of the form<ref name="Quarteroni14"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix} K & B^T \\ B & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf U^{n+1} \\ \mathbf P^{n+1} \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf F^n + \frac{1}{2\delta t}M(4 \mathbf U^n -\mathbf U^{n-1}) \\ \mathbf 0 \end{bmatrix} , \;\;\;\;\;
\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} K & B^T \\ B & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
</math>
where <math display="inline"> K=\frac{3}{2\delta t}M+A+C(U^*) </math>.

==Streamline upwind Petrov–Galerkin formulation for incompressible Navier–Stokes equations==

NS equations with finite element formulation suffer from two source of numerical instability, due to the fact that: 
* NS is a convection dominated problem, which means "large" <math> Re </math>, where numerical oscillations in the velocity field can occur (spurious velocity);
* FE spaces <math> \mathbb{P}_k-\mathbb{P}_k (\forall k) </math> are unstable combinations of velocity and pressure finite element spaces, that do not satisfy the inf-sup condition, and generates numerical oscillations in the pressure field (spurious pressure).

To control instabilities arising from inf-sup condition and convection dominated problem, Pressure-Stabilizing Petrov–Galerkin(PSPG) stabilization along with Streamline-Upwind Petrov–Galerkin (SUPG) stabilization can be added to the NS Galerkin formulation.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

<math display="block">
s(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, p^{n+1}_h ;\mathbf v_h, q_h)=\gamma \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{\mathcal{T}} \int_{\mathcal{T}}\left[ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, p^{n+1}) \right]^T \mathcal{L}_{ss}(\mathbf v_h, q_h)d\mathcal{T},
</math>
where <math> \gamma>0 </math> is a positive constant, <math> \tau_{\mathcal{T}} </math> is a stabilization parameter, <math> \mathcal{T} </math> is a generic tetrahedron belonging to the finite elements [[Graph partition|partitioned]] domain <math> \Omega_h </math>, <math> \mathcal{L}(\mathbf u, p) </math> is the residual of the NS equations.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

<math display="block">
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf u, p) = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}+ (\mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u + \nabla p -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u) \\ \nabla \cdot \mathbf u \end{bmatrix}, 
</math>
and <math> \mathcal{L}_{ss}(\mathbf u, p) </math> is the skew-symmetric part of the NS equations<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>
<math display="block">
\mathcal{L}_{ss}(\mathbf u, p) = \begin{bmatrix}
(\mathbf u \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u + \nabla p \\ \mathbf 0 \end{bmatrix} . 
</math>

The skew-symmetric part of a generic operator <math> \mathcal{L}(\mathbf u, p) </math> is the one for which <math> \Bigl( \mathcal{L}(\mathbf u, p),(\mathbf v, q) \Bigr ) = -\Bigl( (\mathbf v, q), \mathcal{L}(\mathbf u, p) \Bigr ).</math><ref name="Quarteroni07"/>

Since it is based on the residual of the NS equations, the SUPG-PSPG is a strongly [[Numerical method|consistent]] stabilization method.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

The discretized finite element Galerkin formulation with SUPG-PSPG stabilization can be written as:<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

Find, for all <math> t = 0, 1, \ldots, N_t-1, </math> <math>(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,p^{n+1}_h)\in \{ \mathcal{V}_{h} \times \mathcal{Q}_h\} </math>, such that
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&\left( \frac{ 3 \mathbf u_h^{n+1} -4 \mathbf u_h^{n}+ \mathbf u_h^{n-1}}{2\delta t},\mathbf v_h \right) + c(\mathbf u^*_h,\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,\mathbf v_h)+b(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,q_h)-b(\mathbf v_h,p^{n+1}_h) 
\\
& \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; +a(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h,\mathbf v_h)+s(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, p^{n+1}_h ;\mathbf v_h, q_h)=0
\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\forall \mathbf v_h \in \mathcal{V}_{0h} \;\;,\;\; \forall q_h \in \mathcal{Q}_h, 
\end{align}
</math>
with <math> \mathbf{u}^{0}_h=\mathbf{u}_{h,0} </math>, where<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
s(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h, p^{n+1}_h ;\mathbf v_h, q_h) &=\gamma \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} \left( \frac{3 \mathbf u_h^{n+1} -4 \mathbf u_h^{n}+ \mathbf u_h^{n-1}}{2\delta t} 
+ (\mathbf u_h^* \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf u_h^{n+1}+\nabla p^{n+1}_{h}+ \right.
\\
& \left. -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S(\mathbf u^{n+1}_h) \; \boldsymbol{,} \; u_h^* \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h + \frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} 
\right)_{\mathcal{T}}+ \gamma \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{C,\mathcal{T}}\left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf u^{n+1}_h \boldsymbol{,} \; \nabla \cdot \mathbf v_h \right)_{\mathcal{T}}, 
\end{align} 
</math>

and <math> \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} </math>, and <math> \tau_{C,\mathcal{T}} </math> are two stabilization parameters for the momentum and the continuity NS equations, respectively. In addition, the notation <math display="inline"> \left( a \boldsymbol{,} \; b \right)_{\mathcal{T}}=\int_{\mathcal{T}}ab \; d\mathcal{T} </math> has been introduced, and <math> \mathbf u^*_h </math> was defined in agreement with the semi-implicit treatment of the convective term.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

In the previous expression of <math> s \left( \cdot \, ; \cdot \right) </math>, the term <math display="inline"> \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} \left( 
\nabla p^{n+1}_{h} \boldsymbol{,} \; \frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \right)_{\mathcal{T}}, </math> is the Brezzi-Pitkaranta stabilization for the inf-sup, while the term
<math display="inline"> \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} \left( 
u_h^* \cdot \nabla \mathbf u^{n+1}_h \boldsymbol{,} \; u_h^* \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \right)_{\mathcal{T}}, </math>
corresponds to the streamline diffusion term stabilization for large <math> \mathrm{Re} </math>.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/> The other terms occur to obtain a strongly consistent stabilization.<ref name="Tezduyar91"/>

Regarding the choice of the stabilization parameters <math> \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} </math>, and <math> \tau_{C,\mathcal{T}} </math>:<ref name="Tobiska91"/>
<math display="block">
\tau_{M,\mathcal{T}}=\left( \frac{\sigma_{BDF}^2}{\delta t^2} + \frac{\Vert \mathbf u \Vert^2}{h_{\mathcal{T}}^2} + C_k\frac{\nu^2}{h_{\mathcal{T}}^4} \right)^{-1/2}, \;\;\;\;\; \tau_{C,\mathcal{T}}=\frac{h_{\mathcal{T}}^2}{\tau_{M,\mathcal{T}}},
</math>

where: <math> C_k=60 \cdot 2^{k-2} </math> is a constant obtained by an inverse [[Inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] relation (and <math> k </math> is the order of the chosen pair <math> \mathbb{P}_k-\mathbb{P}_k </math>); <math> \sigma_{BDF} </math> is a constant equal to the order of the time discretization; <math> \delta t </math> is the time step; <math> h_{\mathcal{T}} </math> is the "element length" (e.g. the element diameter) of a generic tetrahedra belonging to the partitioned domain <math> \Omega_h </math>.<ref name="Forti15">{{cite journal |last1=Forti |first1=Davide |last2=Dedè |first2=Luca |title=Semi-implicit BDF time discretization of the Navier–Stokes equations with VMS-LES modeling in a High Performance Computing framework |journal=Computers & Fluids |date=August 2015 |volume=117 |pages=168–182 |doi=10.1016/j.compfluid.2015.05.011}}</ref> The parameters <math> \tau_{M,\mathcal{T}} </math> and <math> \tau_{C,\mathcal{T}} </math> can be obtained by a multidimensional generalization of the [[Mathematical optimization|optimal]] value introduced in<ref name="Tezduyar92">{{cite journal |last1=Shih |first1=Rompin |last2=Ray |first2=S. E. |last3=Mittal |first3=Sanjay |last4=Tezduyar |first4=T. E. |title=Incompressible flow computations with stabilized bilinear and linear equal-order-interpolation velocity-pressure elements |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |volume=95 |issue=2 |page=221 |date=1992 |language=en|bibcode=1992CMAME..95..221T |doi=10.1016/0045-7825(92)90141-6 |s2cid=31236394 }}</ref> for the one-dimensional case.<ref name="Tezduyar03">{{cite journal |last1=Kler |first1=Pablo A. |last2=Dalcin |first2=Lisandro D. |last3=Paz |first3=Rodrigo R. |last4=Tezduyar |first4=Tayfun E. |title=SUPG and discontinuity-capturing methods for coupled fluid mechanics and electrochemical transport problems |journal=Computational Mechanics |date=1 February 2013 |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=171–185 |doi=10.1007/s00466-012-0712-z |language=en |issn=1432-0924|bibcode=2013CompM..51..171K |s2cid=123650035 |hdl=11336/1065 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Notice that the terms added by the SUPG-PSPG stabilization can be explicitly written as follows<ref name="Tobiska91"/> 
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
s^{(1)}_{11}=\biggl( \frac{3}{2} \frac{\mathbf u^{n+1}_h}{\delta t} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\;\;\;\;&\;\;\;\; 
s^{(1)}_{21}=\biggl( \frac{3}{2} \frac{\mathbf u^{n+1}_h}{\delta t} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\\
s^{(2)}_{11}=\biggl( \mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf u_h^{n+1} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\;\;\;\;&\;\;\;\;
s^{(2)}_{21}=\biggl( \mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf u_h^{n+1} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\\
s^{(3)}_{11}=\biggl( -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S & (\mathbf u^{n+1}_h) 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\\
s^{(3)}_{21}=\biggl( -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S & (\mathbf u^{n+1}_h) 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\\
s^{(3)}_{11}=\biggl( -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S & (\mathbf u^{n+1}_h) 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\\
s^{(3)}_{21}=\biggl( -2\nu \nabla \cdot \mathbf S & (\mathbf u^{n+1}_h) 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\\
s^{(4)}_{11}=\biggl( \nabla \cdot \mathbf u_h^{n+1} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} & \; 
\nabla \mathbf \cdot \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\end{align}
</math>

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
s_{12}=\biggl( \nabla p_h 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\;\;\;\;&\;\;\;\;
s_{22}=\biggl( \nabla p_h 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\\
f_v=\biggl( \frac{4\mathbf u^{n}_h-\mathbf u^{n-1}_h}{2\delta t} 
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\mathbf u^*_h \cdot \nabla \mathbf v_h \biggr)_\mathcal{T}, 
\;\;\;\;&\;\;\;\; 
f_q=\biggl( \frac{4\mathbf u^{n}_h-\mathbf u^{n-1}_h}{2\delta t}
\; \boldsymbol{,} \; 
\frac{\nabla q_h}{\rho} \biggr)_\mathcal{T},
\end{align}
</math>

where, for the sake of clearness, the sum over the tetrahedra was omitted: all the terms to be intended as <math display="inline"> s^{(n)}_{(I,J)} = \sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \Omega_h} \tau_{\mathcal{T}}\left(\cdot \, , \cdot \right)_\mathcal{T} </math>; moreover, the indices <math> I,J </math> in <math> s^{(n)}_{(I,J)} </math> refer to the position of the corresponding term in the monolithic NS matrix, <math> \Sigma </math>, and <math> n </math> distinguishes the different terms inside each block<ref name="Tobiska91"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
\Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22} \end{bmatrix} \Longrightarrow 
\begin{bmatrix}
s^{(1)}_{(11)} + s^{(2)}_{(11)} + s^{(3)}_{(11)} + s^{(4)}_{(11)} & s_{(12)} \\ s^{(1)}_{(21)}+s^{(2)}_{(21)}+s^{(3)}_{(21)} & s_{(22)} \end{bmatrix} , 
</math>

Hence, the NS monolithic system with the SUPG-PSPG stabilization becomes<ref name="Tobiska91"/>
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
\ \tilde{K} & B^T+S_{12}^T \\ \widetilde{B} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf U^{n+1} \\ \mathbf P^{n+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\ \mathbf F^n + \frac{1}{2\delta t}M(4 \mathbf U^n -\mathbf U^{n-1})+\mathbf F_v \\ \mathbf F_q \end{bmatrix},
</math>
where <math display="inline"> \tilde{K}=K+\sum\limits_{i=1}^4 S^{(i)}_{11} </math>, and <math display="inline"> \tilde{B}=B+\sum\limits_{i=1}^3S^{(i)}_{21} </math>.

It is well known that SUPG-PSPG stabilization does not exhibit excessive numerical diffusion if at least second-order velocity elements and first-order pressure elements (<math> \mathbb{P}_2-\mathbb{P}_1 </math>) are used.<ref name="Tezduyar92"/>


==Goal-Oriented Error Estimation for the Navier–Stokes Equations==
{{AI-section|date=October 2025}}
The goal-oriented approach to finite element error estimation introduces an adjoint (dual) problem whose solution provides a weight function that measures the sensitivity of a functional of interest with respect to the residual of the governing equations.

Incompressible Navier–Stokes Equations

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations (NSE) in an open domain <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3</math>:

<math> \left\{ \begin{aligned} \partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u + \nabla p - \nabla \cdot (\mu \nabla u) &= f, & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],\\ \nabla \cdot u &= 0, & \text{in } \Omega \times (0,T],\\ u &= 0, & \text{on } \partial\Omega \times (0,T],\\ u(x,0) &= u_0(x), & \text{in } \Omega. \end{aligned} \right. </math>
==Linearized Error Equation==

Let <math>(u_h,p_h)</math> be a finite element approximation to <math>(u,p)</math>.
Substitute <math>u = u_h + e_u</math> and <math>p = p_h + e_p</math> into the NSE and subtract the discrete equations satisfied by <math>(u_h,p_h)</math>.
Defining the residual <math>R(\hat{U}_h) = (R_1, R_2)</math>, the (nonlinear) error system becomes

<math> \mathcal{A}(u_h) \begin{pmatrix} e_u \\ e_p \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\,R_1(\hat{U}_h) - (e_u \cdot \nabla)e_u \\[2pt] -\,R_2(\hat{U}_h) \end{pmatrix}, </math>

where the block operators are defined as

<math> \begin{aligned} A_{11}(u_h)[e_u] &= \partial_t e_u + (u_h \cdot \nabla)e_u + (e_u \cdot \nabla)u_h - \nabla\!\cdot(\mu\nabla e_u),\\ A_{12}[e_p] &= \nabla e_p,\\ A_{21}[e_u] &= \nabla\!\cdot e_u,\\ A_{22}[e_p] &= 0. \end{aligned} </math>

The residual components are

<math> \begin{aligned} R_1(\hat{U}_h) &= \partial_t u_h + (u_h \cdot \nabla)u_h - \mu \Delta u_h + \nabla p_h - f,\\ R_2(\hat{U}_h) &= \nabla\!\cdot u_h. \end{aligned} </math>

The linearized error equation can thus be written as

<math> \left\{ \begin{aligned} \partial_t e_u + (u_h \cdot \nabla)e_u + (e_u \cdot \nabla)u_h - \mu \Delta e_u + \nabla e_p &= -\,R_1(\hat{U}_h) - (e_u \cdot \nabla)e_u,\\ \nabla \cdot e_u &= -\,R_2(\hat{U}_h),\\ e_u &= 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega \times (0,T],\\ e_u(x,0) &= 0 \text{ in } \Omega. \end{aligned} \right. </math>
==Adjoint Problem==

To evaluate the error in a specific goal functional

<math> J(u,p) = \int_0^T \!\!\int_\Omega \psi(x,t)\cdot u(x,t)\,dx\,dt, </math>

we introduce adjoint variables <math>\hat{\varphi} = (\varphi_u, \varphi_p)</math> corresponding to the linearized operator.
Integration by parts yields the formal adjoint relation

<math> \langle A_{11}(u_h)e_u + A_{12}e_p,\,\varphi_u\rangle + \langle A_{21}e_u,\,\varphi_p\rangle = \langle e_u,\,A_{11}(u_h)^*\varphi_u + A_{21}^*\varphi_p\rangle + \langle e_p,\,A_{12}^*\varphi_u\rangle. </math>

The corresponding adjoint problem is

<math> \left\{ \begin{aligned} -\,\partial_t \varphi_u - (u_h \cdot \nabla)\varphi_u - (\nabla\!\cdot u_h)\varphi_u + (\nabla u_h)^{T}\varphi_u - \mu \Delta \varphi_u - \nabla \varphi_p &= \psi(x,t), \\ -\nabla \cdot \varphi_u &= 0, \\ \varphi_u &= 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega \times (0,T], \\ \varphi_u(x,T) &= 0 \text{ in } \Omega. \end{aligned} \right. </math>
==Goal-Oriented Error Representation==

The error in the goal functional satisfies

<math> J(u,p) - J(u_h,p_h) = \int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega (u - u_h)\cdot \psi\,dx\,dt = \langle e_u,\,\psi\rangle. </math>

Using the adjoint identity and the adjoint PDE, one finds

<math> \langle e_u,\,\psi\rangle = \langle A_{11}(u_h)e_u + A_{12}e_p,\,\varphi_u\rangle + \langle A_{21}e_u,\,\varphi_p\rangle. </math>

From the nonlinear error equation,

<math> A_{11}(u_h)e_u + A_{12}e_p = -\,R_1(\hat{U}_h) - (e_u\!\cdot\!\nabla)e_u, \qquad A_{21}e_u = -\,R_2(\hat{U}_h). </math>

Neglecting the quadratic term <math>(e_u!\cdot!\nabla)e_u</math> yields the first-order approximation

<math> A_{11}(u_h)e_u + A_{12}e_p \approx -\,R_1(\hat{U}_h), \qquad A_{21}e_u \approx -\,R_2(\hat{U}_h). </math>

Hence,

<math> \langle e_u,\,\psi\rangle \approx -\,\langle R_1(\hat{U}_h),\,\varphi_u\rangle -\,\langle R_2(\hat{U}_h),\,\varphi_p\rangle = -\,\langle R(\hat{U}_h),\,\hat{\varphi}\rangle. </math>

'''Goal-Oriented Error Bound'''

Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality over space–time gives

<math> |J(u,p) - J(u_h,p_h)| \approx |\langle R(\hat{U}_h),\,\hat{\varphi}\rangle| \le \|R(\hat{U}_h)\|\,\|\hat{\varphi}\|. </math>

Thus, the error in the goal functional is bounded by the product of the residual norm and the norm of the adjoint (dual weight) solution:

<math> |J(u,p) - J(u_h,p_h)| \;\lesssim\; \text{Residual of NSE} \times \text{Dual weight}. </math>

This relation forms the basis of goal-oriented adaptive methods, in which the dual solution identifies regions of the computational domain that most strongly influence the functional of interest.
